content.question: In Episode 1 the instructor introduced XML comments. How do you write a comment inside an Android layout XML?

options.text: Use <!-- comment text --> brackets with exclamation and dashes.
Wrap the text with /* comment */ as in Java.
Prefix the line with // to make it a comment.
Use <comment>comment text</comment> element.

content.explanation: The instructor showed using XML comment syntax: <!-- comment --> (an exclamation mark and dashes inside angle brackets) which is ignored by the Android system and improves readability.
hints: He typed brackets, an exclamation mark and four dashes.
This is standard XML comment syntax.
Not Java-style comments.

content.question: To make a layout responsive the instructor set widths to '0dp' and used another attribute. Which attribute controls proportional distribution of space?

options.text: android:layout_weight to assign proportional widths/heights.
android:layout_margin to distribute space proportionally.
android:gravity to divide the screen percentage.
android:padding to allocate percent values.

content.explanation: He explained that using width/height = 0dp combined with android:layout_weight lets child views occupy a percentage of the parent's available space, implementing responsive screens.
hints: He spelled out weight (W-E-I-G-H-T).
Weight expresses a fraction of the parent's available space.
0dp with weight is the common responsive pattern.

content.question: In the example the instructor split a container into 80% and 20%. How did he express 80% using the '10-as-100' trick?

options.text: Use layout_weight='8' for 80% and layout_weight='2' for 20% when total is considered as 10.
Use layout_weight='80' and layout_weight='20' and Android normalizes them automatically.
Set android:widthPercent='80%' directly on the view.
Use layout_weight='4' and layout_weight='1' because weight uses base 5 by default.

content.explanation: He used the shorthand of treating 100% as 10 units, so 80% becomes 8 (layout_weight='8') and 20% becomes 2, giving an 8:2 proportional split.
hints: He said 'we are considering 100 as 10 here'.
80% maps to 8 when using 10 as the base.
Weights are proportional, not absolute pixel values.

content.question: Why did the instructor set button widths to 0dp when using layout_weight for button rows?

options.text: 0dp tells the layout to size the view only based on weight so buttons scale proportionally when the screen stretches.
0dp is required to make buttons invisible on small screens.
0dp sets the button to its intrinsic image size.
0dp disables click events until runtime.

content.explanation: Using 0dp with layout_weight lets the view's size be determined solely by weight, enabling buttons to resize proportionally across different screen widths instead of relying on hardcoded dp sizes.
hints: He repeatedly used 0dp together with weight for responsive buttons.
It prevents hardcoded width from interfering with proportional sizing.
This is a common Android pattern.

content.question: When dividing three equal buttons across a row (100% total), which approximate weight value did the instructor suggest for each when using base 10?

options.text: Use approximately 3.33 (or 3.34) for each button because 100%/3 equals ~33.33 and base 10 converts to ~3.33.
Use weight='1' for each and Android will distribute evenly regardless of base.
Use weight='33' for each and Android will normalize to percent.
Use weight='0' for each when using equal distribution.

content.explanation: He explained dividing 100 by 3 yields ~33.33%; treating 100 as 10 gives ~3.33 per button (or 3.34), which approximates equal distribution when using weights on a 0dp width setup.
hints: He described converting 33.33 to 3.33 for the base-10 trick.
Weights express proportions; small decimals are acceptable here.
This was shown when creating three buttons per row.

content.question: Which attribute did the instructor set to add outside spacing between buttons in the numeric rows?

options.text: android:layout_margin (e.g., 7dp) to create outer gaps between buttons.
android:padding to create outer gaps between buttons.
android:src to space buttons by drawable.
android:alpha to fade gaps into visibility.

content.explanation: He used margin (7dp) to give outer spacing between adjacent buttons — margin controls outside spacing between sibling views.
hints: He set margin=7dp when creating buttons.
Margin is for external spacing, padding is internal.
This improves visual separation and touch targets.

content.question: What background color resource name did the instructor repeatedly apply to number and operator buttons in Episode 1?

options.text: vivid_green
pastel_blue
text_blue
background_white

content.explanation: He set the button background to vivid_green for the numeric and operator buttons in the demo.
hints: He said 'Background will be vivid green'.
It was used consistently for buttons.

content.question: When arranging operator buttons vertically, the instructor used 0dp for height and weights to split space. He allocated 60% to four operators and 40% to the 'equals' button. If 100% is treated as 10, what weight did he assign the 'equals' group?

options.text: 4 (since 40% maps to 4 when 100% is treated as 10).
6 (because 60% goes to operators).
1 (default weight).
0 (equals should have fixed height).

content.explanation: He used an 60/40 split; treating 100 as 10 makes 40% correspond to weight='4', so the equals group used weight 4 while the four operators shared weight 6.
hints: He explicitly said 60% for four and 40% for equals.
Recall the base-10 conversion trick.

content.question: The instructor initially saw an 'abnormality' when a container used wrap_content in a percent-based context. What did he change to fix it?

options.text: Changed the container's height from wrap_content to match_parent to eliminate the abnormality.
Switched all children to fixed dp values to stabilize layout.
Removed all margins so the layout recalculated correctly.
Converted the LinearLayout to ConstraintLayout to fix the issue.

content.explanation: He discovered wrap_content caused the container to expand with its contents and conflict with percent allocations; switching to match_parent fixed the abnormality so percent/weight calculations worked as intended.
hints: He said the problem was wrap_content and he set match_parent to fix it.
Match_parent gives the container the expected reference size for percentage splits.

content.question: Which small visual adjustment did the instructor make to the 'equals' button to match the design after changing margins and heights?

options.text: He adjusted marginBottom (e.g., between 20dp and 17dp) to fine-tune appearance.
He changed the equals button text to 'Enter' to match the mock-up.
He removed the background color from the equals button.
He rotated the equals button by 90 degrees.

content.explanation: He iteratively adjusted marginBottom (testing 20dp, 18dp, 17dp) to get the final visual spacing for the equals button to match the mock-up.
hints: He tried 20, 18, 19, then settled on 17 dp.
This was a final visual tweak, not a functional change.
